title: LiLiCorr: Lightweight Likelihood Correlation of Parallel Drafts for Speculative Decoding

# LiLiCorr: Lightweight Likelihood Correlation of Parallel Drafts for Speculative Decoding

Matan Rusanovsky $^{*}$ Yoav Miron Roy Uziel Omer Belhasin Hao Guo Ran Zilberstein Maor Ashkenazi Michael Elad

NVIDIA

## Abstract

Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by drafting future tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. A diffusion-style drafter, such as DFlash, drafts an entire block in one forward pass. It is trained on the per-position marginals rather than on the joint distribution over the block, so the tokens it emits are individually plausible yet jointly incoherent. We introduce LiLiCorr, a Lightweight Likelihood-based model that Corrrelates the per-position marginal distributions such a drafter produces. It keeps the top- $K$ tokens at each position as candidates and processes them jointly, producing for each an in and an out vector. A pair at consecutive positions matches when the earlier candidate's out vector aligns, in cosine similarity, with the later one's in vector. Training makes the correct pairings score highest while pushing competing ones down, so coherent blocks outscore incoherent ones. The joint distribution over the block, exponential in its length, is never materialized. One lightweight network pass produces all the vectors, and the pairwise scores follow as batched matrix operations, leaving only a cheap greedy walk sequential. We co-train the DFlash drafter with LiLiCorr, so it learns to propose candidates that correlate into longer accepted sequences. Over the vanilla DFlash drafter it builds on, LiLiCorr accepts more and serves faster at every one of the 72 settings we test: nine benchmarks at two target sizes under greedy and temperature-one decoding, together with a throughput sweep over six concurrencies, two input lengths and three output-entropy tiers. It raises acceptance length by 7 to 19%, while its single-pass scoring head accounts for only about 3% of the per-block latency. Against three concurrently developed methods that also restore coherence at draft time, every system equally optimized on a common serving stack, LiLiCorr holds the highest throughput in 63 of those settings, ties within a measured noise floor in 6, and trails in only 3.

## 1 Introduction

## 1 Introduction

Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive language-model inference by letting a small draft model propose several future tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, keeping the longest correct prefix (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). Because decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, verifying a multitude of tokens together costs little more than generating just one token. The resulting speedup depends on two quantities: the acceptance length, the expected number of draft tokens accepted per step, and the cost of the drafter itself. A good drafter must raise the former without inflating the latter. Much effort therefore goes into raising acceptance length, with designs ranging from feature-autoregressive heads such as EAGLE (Li et al., 2024a;b; 2026) to multi-head predictors such as Medusa (Cai et al., 2024). A particularly promising approach predicts an entire block of future tokens in a single forward pass via a parallel diffusion-style drafter, such as DFlash (Chen et al., 2026), offering a long speculative window at very low cost.

In this work we build on DFlash, which predicts an entire block of future tokens in one forward pass. For each position in the block, henceforth a slot, it produces a distribution over the full vocabulary. Although DFlash attends bidirectionally across slots, so its representations can in principle correlate

This marginals problem is well known in the discrete diffusion literature, and its origin is combinatorial: the joint distribution over a block of B positions, each drawn from a vocabulary of size V, has $V^{B}$ possible realizations, so materializing it is intractable even for very short blocks. Diffusion language models therefore never model the joint explicitly, and both diffusion and speculative-decoding literature offer ways to recover coherence without it. Masked diffusion models such as LLaDA, MDLM, and Dream (Nie et al., 2026; Sahoo et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2025) correlate the sequence through iterative denoising, re-masking a subset of the predicted tokens and re-predicting them over several rounds. In a speculative-decoding setting, however, each such round is another full drafter pass, which is too expensive. Tree-based reranking, such as DDTree (Ringel and Romano, 2026), expands several candidate paths from the per-slot marginals and lets the target model select among them. This shifts the correlation work onto the target, whose passes speculative decoding is designed to save. The trade is especially unfavorable in the compute-bound, high-concurrency regime typical of real-world serving. In contrast, Domino (Huang et al., 2026) and DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026), two works concurrent with ours, act at draft time while avoiding extra target passes, but they do so through a sequence of auto-regressive neural-network passes, one on each draft slot. A third work developed concurrently with ours, DFlash2 (Inco AI, 2026), avoids the per-slot pass, scoring each adjacent pair of tokens from learned embeddings of their two identities. Compatibility is therefore a property of the token pair itself rather than of the draft it appears in: the same two tokens score alike in every context.

We introduce LiLiCorr, a lightweight likelihood-based model that recovers a coherent sequence from the per-slot marginals in a single network pass. Figure 1 sets out the method end to end. LiLiCorr takes the top- K candidate tokens at each slot and produces two vectors per candidate: in and out. These capture how candidates chain together: two adjacent candidates are compatible when the out vector of the first aligns, in cosine similarity, with the in vector of the second. Training aligns the out and in vectors of consecutive ground-truth tokens and separates the competing pairings. At inference, a cheap greedy walk commits the block left to right, at each position taking the candidate that best matches its committed predecessor. The novelty is that every vector is produced in a single pass over all candidates at all slots, so each pair is scored in the light of the candidates around it, at the slots before it and after it. Correlation then reduces to matrix operations that are easy to optimize, all candidate interactions computed in parallel, with only the greedy path selection left sequential. Approaches that correct one slot at a time instead run their network at every position.

LiLiCorr is trained jointly with DFlash rather than on top of a frozen drafter, so the drafter learns to propose candidate sets that LiLiCorr can turn into longer accepted sequences. Against a vanilla

DFlash drafter trained on the same data, this raises acceptance length by 7 to 19% on every benchmark, for 8B and 4B target sizes and both greedy and temperature-1 decoding. We also compare against the three works above, Domino, DSpark and DFlash2, which likewise tune the drafter alongside their head, giving every system the same optimization effort on a common serving stack. LiLiCorr is the fastest system at almost every setting we measure, and most of the few exceptions sit inside the measurement noise. Against the two systems that correct one slot at a time the advantage is structural, since they spend a network pass per slot where LiLiCorr scores every candidate at once. Against DFlash2, which also drafts in one pass, the difference lies in the scoring rule. DFlash2 scores a pair from the identities of its two tokens, so the same pair scores alike in every draft, whereas every LiLiCorr score is formed from vectors that have seen every candidate at every slot. This structural difference yields longer accepted prefixes, on average at both target sizes and under both decoding regimes. The lead persists as concurrency rises.

## Contributions.

(1) A novel likelihood-based formulation of the marginals problem. We cast the recovery of a coherent sequence from per-slot marginals as a learned scoring model over candidate paths. Rather than reason in the full vocabulary, the model attends over all candidates of all slots by assigning two low-dimensional vectors to each, which encode how neighbors are matched.

(2) Correlation as efficient parallel matrix operations. At decoding time, a single network pass precomputes all of the correlations, as the pairwise candidate interactions reduce to matrix operations that are easy to optimize. This is followed by a cheap greedy walk that remains sequential.

(3) State-of-the-art results. LiLiCorr sets a new state-of-the-art for draft-time correlation in speculative decoding, trained jointly with the drafter and given the same data, training budget, and optimization effort as the three concurrent works Huang et al. (2026); Cheng et al. (2026); Inco AI (2026). We evaluate on nine benchmarks, at two target sizes and under both greedy and temperature-one decoding, and on a throughput sweep over six serving concurrencies, two input lengths, and three output-entropy tiers. LiLiCorr holds the highest throughput of any system compared in 63 of these 72 settings, ties within a measured noise floor in 6 and trails in only 3.

## 2 Related Work

## 2 Related Work

Speculative decoding and parallel drafters. Speculative decoding accelerates inference by proposing draft tokens and verifying them with the target model under a rule that preserves its distribution (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). Most work along these lines improves the drafter, from multi-head predictors such as Medusa (Cai et al., 2024) to feature-autoregressive heads such as the EAGLE family (Li et al., 2024a;b; 2026). A separate line of work drafts an entire block in one forward pass: parallel and diffusion-style block heads such as DFlash (Chen et al., 2026) and diffusion-based self-speculation (Fu et al., 2026) handle a long speculative window cheaply. D-PACE (Wu et al., 2026) improves DFlash with an acceptance-aware training objective. Their parallel prediction mirrors that of diffusion language models, such as LLaDA (Nie et al., 2026), MDLM (Sahoo et al., 2024), Dream (Ye et al., 2025), and Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion (Fu et al., 2026). These models exhibit a well-known marginals limitation: although attention is bidirectional, the block is factorized into independent per-position predictions, so the sampled tokens are not guaranteed to be jointly coherent. This is addressed via an iterative refinement, re-masking and re-predicting subsets of tokens so that later rounds condition on earlier ones. Parallel drafters inherit the same limitation, but in speculative decoding each refinement round adds a full drafter pass, which negates the latency gains that motivate parallel drafting. Recovering coherence without repeated drafter passes is the problem LiLiCorr addresses.

Recovering coherent drafts. Several recent methods recover a coherent sequence from the perslot marginals that a parallel drafter such as DFlash produces. One direction expands these marginals into a draft tree of several continuations that the target verifies in a single pass. DDTree (Ringel and Romano, 2026) is training-free, ranking candidate prefixes by their marginal product, whereas Oda et al. (2026) first learn a small autoregressive adapter before building the tree. Both push the correlation work onto the target, spending the compute speculative decoding aims to save, and both rely on tree-structured attention, which is typically less efficient than standard causal attention.

An alternative direction reintroduces the dependencies at draft time: Domino (Huang et al., 2026) and DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026), two of the works developed concurrently with ours, condition each slot on the previously sampled tokens, which avoids extra target passes but runs a correction network once at every slot. A third work developed concurrently with ours, DFlash2 (Inco AI, 2026), correlates the block without such a per-slot pass. It learns two embedding tables over the vocabulary, one holding a vector for each token as a predecessor and one for each token as a successor, and scores a pair of neighboring tokens by the inner product of the two. The score is added to the drafter's logits, and the block is filled left to right, each slot committing the candidate that scores best against the token just committed. What a pair receives is therefore fixed by the identities of its two tokens, the same score in every draft. DFlash2 introduces a second and independent contribution, a grouped causal convolution inside each draft layer that lets neighboring slots exchange local information while the block stays parallel. The convolution acts on the drafter rather than on the correlation, so the two compose, and we ablate it on top of LiLiCorr in Appendix C. The marginals problem is not unique to speculative decoding: non-autoregressive translation meets it in the same form, and Sun et al. (2019) correlate a parallel decoder by factorizing adjacent-pair scores into per-token vectors over a top-$K$ pool. What differs here is that speculative decoding credits only an accepted prefix, which is why LiLiCorr normalizes each slot locally and commits greedily rather than decoding the best-scoring path. LiLiCorr also acts at draft time and in a single pass: it produces all candidate representations at once, computes their pairwise correlations in parallel, and leaves only a cheap greedy argmax over the resulting scores to run sequentially. Its vectors are formed from every candidate in the block, so the score of a pair reflects the context of the entire draft rather than the two token identities alone.

## 3 Method

## 3.1 Setup: prefix acceptance and the marginal drafter

## 3 Method

## 3.1 Setup: prefix acceptance and the marginal drafter

Let M be a frozen target language model. A parallel block drafter proposes, in a single forward pass, a block of B positions conditioned on the verified context, of which $B-1$ are future tokens. The first block position is the last token the target has committed, which serves as the anchor, slot 0. The remaining $B-1$ positions are the speculative slots 1,..., $B-1$. At each slot the drafter produces a distribution (logit) over the vocabulary, a per-slot marginal. Standard decoding resolves each slot independently, taking its most probable token. Once the draft is complete, the target verifies the whole block in a single pass and accepts a prefix of it, discarding everything from the first rejected position onward. With a greedy target a draft token is accepted when it coincides with the target's own choice. Under a sampling target, acceptance instead follows the standard rejection test, which preserves the target distribution exactly (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). In both regimes acceptance is prefix-structured, and it is this structure that LiLiCorr is built around.

## 3.2 A scoring model over the candidate lattice

## 3.2 A scoring model over the candidate lattice

The drafter is supervised on per-slot marginals, so the tokens it selects are individually probable but not necessarily compatible with one another. Selecting tokens that are jointly compatible, and not only locally probable, can lengthen the accepted prefix, and doing so at draft time could avoid extra target passes. LiLiCorr addresses this goal by correlating the slots over a small pool of alternatives that the drafter's own marginal already places near the top. At each slot s it retains the drafter's top- K candidate tokens $c_{s,1},\dots,c_{s,K}$ rather than its single most probable one. Each candidate is a token, and we represent it by a vector we call its node, formed by summing four terms of equal width: the target's frozen input embedding of the token, the drafter's hidden state at that slot, a small network over a few scalar features of how confident the drafter is in that candidate, listed in Appendix A, and learned encodings of the slot and of the candidate's rank. The hidden state belongs to the slot and is shared by its K candidates, so what separates them is the token itself, its confidence, and its rank. Across the B-1 slots these nodes form a $(B-1)\times K$ lattice.

A small Transformer processes the $( B-1 ) \times K$ nodes jointly. Its self-attention lets every candidate exchange information with every other, both the competing candidates within a slot and the candidates at neighboring slots, so each is represented in the context of the whole block rather than on its own. Each attended node is then fused with a projection of the target's hidden state that produced the last verified token: the candidate's own state, that projection, and their elementwise product are

concatenated and mapped back to the node width by a single layer. Though one vector common to the whole block, it enters every candidate separately, so that the verifier's view of the context, and not the drafter's alone, shapes each of them. For each node LiLiCorr emits two vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}$ , an out vector o and an in vector i, each normalized to unit norm. The dimension $d_{e}$ is given in Appendix A. The anchor, which precedes the first slot, is encoded far more thinly: the anchor projection itself, mapped by its own head to one further out vector. Indexing the anchor as slot 0, we write this vector $\mathbf{o}_{0}$ . Adjacent slots s and s+1 are then coupled by a single matching term, the cosine similarity between the out and in vectors:

$$
\phi^ {\mathrm {p}} \left(s, k, k ^ {\prime}\right) = \sigma \cos \left(\mathbf {o} _ {s, k}, \mathbf {i} _ {s + 1, k ^ {\prime}}\right) \quad \mathrm {f o r} \quad s = 0, \dots , B - 2, \quad 1 \leq k \leq K _ {s}, 1 \leq k ^ {\prime} \leq K,
$$

(1)

where $\cos(\cdot, \cdot)$ is the cosine similarity and $\sigma$ is a fixed scaling constant, with $K_{0}=1$ at the anchor, which carries a single out vector, and $K_{s}=K$ at every speculative slot. Figure 1(b) shows the lattice and the pair of vectors each candidate carries.

The factorization is local, but the information behind it is not. Only adjacent slots are coupled by a score, yet the vectors that form that score depend on the entire lattice, so a pair at slots s and s+1 may be judged compatible on evidence lying outside them, among the candidates that precede s or follow s+1. We hypothesize that this is the more useful place to spend capacity: rather than enrich the coupling itself, we keep it pairwise and let the vectors it multiplies see the whole block. The pairwise form is what leaves the scores computable as batched matrix products.

Casting each score as a cosine is a deliberate stabilizer: it removes vector magnitude as an unconstrained degree of freedom. Without this bound we observe runaway score magnitudes that corrupt, and in practice destroy, the shared DFlash backbone under joint training. The cosine instead confines every learned factor to $[-\sigma, \sigma]$ while avoiding saturating nonlinearities whose gradients vanish. We use a fixed scale $\sigma$ to separate the candidate scores to discriminate among them. Its value, and the architecture of the head, are given in Appendix A.

## 3.3 Training the reranker

Local normalization aligned with prefix acceptance. A natural formulation scores each full path by summing its matching terms across the block and selects the path that maximizes this wholechain score. We argue that this is the wrong target under prefix acceptance. The global optimum may sacrifice an early slot to win a richer tail, yet under prefix acceptance that tail is never reached. Section 3.5 and Appendix F take up this comparison at decoding time. Optimizing the whole chain thus spends capacity on regions the metric never credits. We therefore score each slot locally, conditioned on the candidate committed just before it. Writing the per-slot node score of candidate k as $z_{s}[k]$ , the chain rule factorizes the path distribution as

$$
P _ {\theta} \left(c _ {s} \mid c _ {s - 1}\right) = \operatorname {s o f t m a x} _ {k} \left(z _ {s} [ k ]\right), \quad z _ {s} [ k ] = \phi^ {\mathrm {p}} \left(s - 1, c _ {s - 1}, k\right), \quad s = 1, \dots , B - 1,
$$

(2)

where $c_{s}$ is the candidate committed at slot s and $c_{0}$ is the anchor. Each conditional still depends on the previous pick through the matching term in $z_{s}[k]$ , so locality avoids scoring the whole chain without reducing the model to a per-slot reranker.

Oracle-prefix supervision. We train LiLiCorr as a teacher-forced reranker over the drafter's marginals, so the supervision must reflect how it is served. Two conditions decide which slots carry a learning signal. The first is coverage: a slot is useful only when its ground-truth token is among the drafter's K candidates, since otherwise no reranking can recover it. The second follows from prefix acceptance. We condition each transition on the ground-truth predecessor $g_{s-1}$ : a path that has already left the ground truth is discarded by the verifier, so the transitions leaving it are never exercised in serving. A slot is therefore supervised only when every earlier slot is covered as well. Together these define the oracle prefix, the longest leading run of slots that each contain the ground-truth token among their K candidates. Let S collect these slots across a training batch. We teacher-force the per-slot cross-entropy on them:

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {C E}} = - \frac {1}{| \mathcal {S} |} \sum_ {s \in \mathcal {S}} \log P _ {\theta} \left(c _ {s} = g _ {s} \mid c _ {s - 1} = g _ {s - 1}\right),
$$

(3)

where $g_{s}$ is the ground-truth token at slot s. The softmax of Eq. (2) runs over all K candidates at slot s, so each supervised transition raises the ground-truth successor and pushes its K-1 competitors

down. A block whose very first slot already misses contributes zero loss. The effect resembles the per-slot decay used to train DFlash, though it arises from the coverage mask rather than from a designed weighting: supervision concentrates on earlier slots.

Target-weighted distractor penalty. The per-slot cross-entropy raises the ground-truth probability but is indifferent to how the residual mass is distributed among the remaining candidates. Under cross-entropy supervision alone, we observed that LiLiCorr's errors were typically candidates the target scored well-below the ground truth, a mismatch with the verifier rather than a genuine ambiguity in the target distribution. Since the target is itself the verifier, its logits provide a graded measure of candidate compatibility that cross-entropy ignores. Scoring against the target lets us direct the negative gradient at these high-scoring but target-incompatible competitors, widening the ground truth's margin over the candidates most likely to trigger an early verification failure.

Let $q_{k}$ denote the target probability of candidate k, and $g_{s}$ the ground-truth candidate at slot s. Both $q_{g_{s}}$ and the $q_{k}$ are indexed out of the teacher-forced target pass that already supplies the drafter's supervision. We define

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {d i s t}} = \frac {1}{| \mathcal {S} |} \sum_ {s \in \mathcal {S}} \Omega_ {s}, \quad \Omega_ {s} = \sum_ {k} P _ {\theta} \left(c _ {s} = k \mid c _ {s - 1} = g _ {s - 1}\right) \mathrm {R e L U} \left(\log q _ {g _ {s}} - \log q _ {k}\right),
$$

(4)

(4)

where $\Omega_{s}$ is the target-relative cost LiLiCorr expects to pay at slot s under its own distribution, which are averaged over the supervised slots in $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{d i s t}}$ . Candidates the target ranks below $g_{s}$ are penalized in proportion to the gap, and those it ranks above are not penalized at all. When $g_{s}$ is the target's top candidate, this term shares its gradient with a target cross-entropy over the candidate pool, and the rectifier extends it safely to the rare positions where $g_{s}$ is not the target's top candidate, as detailed in Appendix E.

We keep it alongside the hard cross-entropy because the two supply complementary gradients. Cross-entropy makes LiLiCorr rank the ground truth first even when the target assigns it only modest probability, so it remains the selected token however soft the target is. The distractor penalty complements this by pushing the confusers the target disfavors further down. It is therefore cost-aware shaping of cross-entropy, not a replacement, as detailed in Appendix E.

## 3.4 Co-adapting the drafter and the reranker

We tune DFlash jointly with LiLiCorr, so that the drafter learns to expose candidate pools and hidden representations from which LiLiCorr can assemble longer accepted prefixes. Joint training must cross the top- $K$ selection that forms the candidate pool, which is not differentiable. We keep the selected candidate indices fixed and retain gradients through their draft log-probabilities and the hidden states from which they were produced, $^{1}$ both of which are inputs to LiLiCorr. The acceptance-oriented loss therefore reaches the DFlash backbone without differentiating pool membership, and inference is unchanged.

The drafter keeps its own DFlash training loss, a per-slot block cross-entropy over the drafter marginals that weights earlier slots more heavily (Chen et al., 2026),

$$
\mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {D F l a s h}} = - \sum_ {s = 1} ^ {B - 1} w _ {s} \log p _ {s} \left(g _ {s}\right), \quad w _ {s} = \exp \left(- \frac {s - 1}{\beta}\right),
$$

(5)

(5)

where $p_{s}$ is the drafter's marginal at slot s and $\beta$ sets the decay. The drafter and LiLiCorr are trained jointly to minimize the drafter loss together with the two reranker terms,

$$
\mathcal {L} = \mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {D F l a s h}} + \gamma \left[ \mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {C E}} + \lambda \mathcal {L} _ {\mathrm {d i s t}} \right].
$$

(6)

Here $\gamma$ sets the weight of the reranker objective as a whole and $\lambda$ scales the distractor penalty within it. These weights and the decay $\beta$ are given in Appendix A. Appendix D ablates the distractor penalty at a fixed objective weight: it raises acceptance length on all nine benchmarks, and by 1.5% on the average.

$^{1}$ The candidate token embeddings remain frozen.

## 3.5 Single-pass decoding

Decoding has a parallel- and a sequential stage, and the network runs only once. In the parallel stage, a single LiLiCorr pass produces every outgoing and incoming vector, including the anchor out vector. The block has $B-1$ adjacent slot pairs, and within each pair every candidate is matched against every candidate in the next slot. This gives $K^{2}$ comparisons for each of the $B-2$ interior pairs and K for the anchor pair, $(B-2)K^{2}+K$ matching terms in total. Evaluating them reduces to one matrix multiplication per slot pair, batched across the full block, which keeps the computation static in shape and well suited to kernel fusion and graph capture. In the sequential stage, the block is committed greedily from left to right: at slot s we select

$$
\hat {c} _ {s} = \underset {k} {\arg \max } z _ {s} [ k ] = \underset {k} {\arg \max } \phi^ {\mathrm {p}} (s - 1, \hat {c} _ {s - 1}, k),
$$

(7)

conditioning each slot on the candidate just committed, a walk traced in Figure 1(c). This greedy rule is exactly the inference behavior the local objective in Eq. (2) was trained to optimize. An alternative is to commit the path that maximizes the sum of the matching terms. Appendix F recovers that path exactly with a dynamic program and finds it decodes worse than the greedy rule. Only the argmax walk is sequential, and it touches no network weights; the expensive computation is the single parallel pass. This is the key distinction from iterative-refinement drafters, which invoke a network once per position: LiLiCorr confines all learning to one pass and reduces the per-position work to an argmax over precomputed matching scores.

## 4 Experiments

## 4.1 Experimental setup

## 4 Experiments

## 4.1 Experimental setup

Models and evaluation. We use frozen Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B targets (Yang et al., 2025) with their reasoning mode disabled. Evaluation spans eight public datasets across three domains: math (GSM8K, MATH-500, AIME 2025), code (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench), and chat (Alpaca, MT-Bench). We additionally report on SPEED-Bench (Abramovich et al., 2026), hereafter SPEED, whose qualitative split holds 880 prompts across eleven categories. We evaluate two decoding regimes: a deterministic one with a greedy target, and a sampling one at temperature 1 over the untruncated target distribution, verified by exact rejection sampling so that the target distribution is preserved and averaged over three seeds. We measure the acceptance length $\tau$ , computed block-weighted as the total number of accepted tokens divided by the number of verification blocks, together with output throughput and the resulting speedup over the target's own autoregressive decoding on the same hardware. Three ablations are deferred to Appendices D, F and C: the distractor penalty, the greedy decode rule, and DFlash2's convolution placed in the DFlash backbone that precedes LiLiCorr.

Baselines. We compare LiLiCorr against three concurrent works to ours, Domino Huang et al. (2026), DSpark Cheng et al. (2026) and DFlash2 Inco AI (2026), and against the DFlash drafter it builds on. All three tune the DFlash drafter as they train their own head, as LiLiCorr does. DFlash2's convolution acts on the drafter rather than on the correlation head, so the two compose, and we ablate it on top of LiLiCorr in Appendix C. At temperature 1 the verifier's rejection-sampling step reproduces the target distribution however the block was drafted, so a drafter is free either to commit each slot to its own argmax or to sample its proposal. Domino and DFlash only take the argmax, whereas LiLiCorr, DSpark and DFlash2 do both. Table 1 reports the sampled proposal where a system has one and the argmax otherwise, and Table 7 reports every system under the argmax. All systems are trained on the same corpus, for the same number of epochs and at the same global batch size and sequence length, under an identical configuration across systems and target sizes, so acceptance length and throughput are directly comparable.

Implementation details. We serve every system on the same deployment-representative SGLang backend, with block size 16 on a single H100 and concurrency one unless stated otherwise. Every speculative head is folded into the drafter and optimized with fused kernels and graph capture. Fully optimized, the LiLiCorr head costs 0.299 ms per block, against Domino's 0.611 and DSpark's 0.779, and accounts for about 3% of the per-block wall on Qwen3-8B and 4.5% on the cheaper Qwen3-4B

Acceptance length is reproducible to the digits we print, but throughput is not: repeated runs of one system on one node at concurrency one differ by up to 0.94% . We therefore set the noise floor at 1%, reading a throughput difference of at most that as a tie and counting a win only where a system leads every other by more.

Training data. All systems are trained on roughly 1.4M examples drawn from the code, mathematics, STEM, and general-chat splits of the Nemotron Post-Training Dataset V2 (Nathawani et al., 2025), with the multilingual splits excluded and every assistant turn regenerated with the target model (Appendix A).

## 4.2 Main results

Table 1 reports speedup over autoregressive decoding on the nine benchmarks, for both target sizes and both decoding regimes; the acceptance lengths and absolute throughputs behind it are deferred to Appendix B. The four draft-time methods reach comparable acceptance lengths, so throughput separates them. Under greedy decoding LiLiCorr is fastest in twelve of the eighteen settings, ties in four and trails in two, both deficits being HumanEval against DFlash2. Against the DFlash drafter, which reranks nothing, LiLiCorr improves on both axes everywhere, raising acceptance length by 13 to 19% and throughput by 6 to 14%. Tables 8 and 9 resolve SPEED into its eleven categories, in all forty-four of which LiLiCorr serves faster than every system compared, and by its widest acceptance margin on multilingual. It is the only domain held out of training, which suggests a capacity to generalize out of distribution.

Sampling does not reorder the systems. At temperature one accepted prefixes shorten for every system, as expected once the target no longer commits to its own argmax. Among argmax proposals LiLiCorr is fastest at all eighteen settings, and among sampled ones at fifteen, tying at two and trailing at one. DSpark accepts longer prefixes than LiLiCorr at 8B, by 3.1% on the sampled average, and still serves slower: our cheaper head completes 7.2% more verification blocks per second, which more than offsets the shorter prefix (Table 5).

## 4.3 Scaling with concurrency

Deployed systems run batched, a regime in which decoding moves from memory-bandwidth bound towards compute bound and the cost of speculation is weighed differently. SPEED provides a second, throughput split for this setting, which holds the input length fixed, generates 1,024 tokens per request and varies serving concurrency (Abramovich et al., 2026). We evaluate on its 1K and 2K input-length blocks, in each of their three output-entropy tiers. The tiers group prompts by how predictable their continuations are: coding and mathematics sit in the low-entropy tier and are easier to draft, roleplay and writing in the high-entropy tier and are harder. Every drafter is trained on sequences of 3,120 tokens (Table 4), and these are the two blocks whose input and generation together stay within that length.

## 5 Conclusion

## 5 Conclusion

LiLiCorr correlates the per-slot marginals of a parallel block drafter in a single network pass. Assigning each candidate an in and an out vector reduces the correlation to batched matrix products,

leaving only a greedy walk that touches no network weights. Trained jointly with the drafter, LiLiCorr improves on the vanilla DFlash drafter on every benchmark we test, and a draft of comparable quality at a fraction of the cost of correcting one slot at a time makes it the faster system almost everywhere we measure.

One limitation is inherent to the design: LiLiCorr reranks only the top- $K$ tokens the drafter proposes, so a slot whose correct token is absent from that pool cannot be recovered, and the achievable acceptance length is bounded by the drafter's coverage. A second follows from scoring the block through adjacent pairs alone. Each candidate is represented from the whole block, so evidence from distant slots reaches a pair score, but only after being compressed into that one number. Coupling distant slots explicitly is a natural next step, and whether it repays its cost remains open.
